Guided demo

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 28: Magnetic Forces and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional illustration of a positively charged particle following a helical path in a uniform magnetic field. Three axes meet at the origin O, with x running to the right, y upward, and z toward the lower left, and a small orange sphere labeled q sits at the origin. From the particle, a green arrow labeled 'v perp' points straight up along y, a short arrow labeled 'v para' points along the x direction, and a green arrow labeled 'v' between the two gives the total velocity. A blue arrow labeled with a vector B lies along the positive x-axis, and a red arrow labeled 'F' is drawn at the particle. An orange helix of roughly three turns occupies the right side of the frame, each loop circling in the plane perpendicular to x with small arrowheads on the coils marking the sense of rotation, and successive loops shifted steadily in the positive x direction. Above the coils a short green double-headed arrow labeled 'v para' spans the gap between two consecutive turns. Splitting the velocity into two components makes visible which part bends the trajectory and which part carries the particle forward. The drawing shows how a velocity oblique to the field yields circular motion superposed on uniform travel along it.

elements: Three coordinate axes meeting at origin O: +x arrow to screen-right (long, horizontal), +y arrow straight up, +z arrow toward lower-left (short diagonal)
Axis labels 'x', 'y', 'z' at arrow tips and 'O' at the origin
Small orange sphere (the charge) at the origin, labeled 'q' just below it
Green arrow v_perp pointing straight up along +y from the particle, labeled 'v⃗_perp'
Short green arrow v_para pointing along +x from the particle, labeled 'v⃗_para' (label below the x-axis)
Green arrow v⃗ (resultant velocity) between v_perp and v_para, tilted up-right, labeled 'v⃗'
Red arrow F⃗ at the particle, shorter, pointing up-right toward the helix interior (magnetic force, qv×B), labeled 'F⃗'
Blue arrow B⃗ lying along the +x axis just right of the particle, labeled 'B⃗'
Orange helix of ~3 turns, axis along +x, loops drawn as ellipses in planes perpendicular to x, successive loops shifted in +x
Small orange arrowheads on the coils indicating the sense of rotation
Short green double-headed arrow above the coils spanning one pitch (gap between two consecutive turns), labeled 'v_para'
Moving particle dot that traces the helix during the animation (trail of the path)

interactions.teaches: The helix is a circle in the y–z plane carried steadily along x; rotating the view shows the trajectory is truly three-dimensional, not a wavy 2D curve.
The perpendicular velocity component makes the particle circle the field line while the parallel component carries it forward at constant speed, producing a helix.
interactions.label: Launch particle

interactions.teaches: Increasing the velocity component along B stretches the pitch (spacing between turns) while leaving the loop radius and rotation period unchanged.
interactions.label: v_parallel (along B)

interactions.teaches: The perpendicular component sets the gyroradius r = m·v_perp/(qB) and the tangential speed, but never the axial advance per turn's period.
interactions.label: v_perpendicular (across B)

demo_steps.title: Velocity split into two components
demo_steps.narration: The charge q at the origin has velocity v⃗ oblique to B⃗, which points along +x. Decompose it: v_perp up along y, v_para along x.

demo_steps.title: Perpendicular part alone → circle
demo_steps.narration: With v_para set to zero, the magnetic force F = qv×B stays perpendicular to the motion and the particle traces a closed circle in the plane perpendicular to B.

demo_steps.title: Add forward motion → helix
demo_steps.narration: Restoring v_para carries the circling particle steadily along the field line; the circle becomes a helix whose pitch is v_para times the cyclotron period.

demo_steps.title: Stretching the pitch
demo_steps.narration: Doubling v_para doubles the spacing between turns while the loop radius stays exactly the same — forward speed alone sets the pitch.

demo_steps.title: Widening the gyration
demo_steps.narration: Raising v_perp enlarges the loop radius and the speed around it, but the period — and therefore the pitch — is unchanged.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: +X is screen-right (the x-axis and B direction), +Y is screen-up, +Z recedes toward the lower-left. x-axis drawn from -0.8 to +6.0 with arrowhead at right; y-axis from 0 to +3.2; z-axis from 0 to about +2.0 projected toward lower-left (shorter than the others). Origin O at world (0,0,0) with an orange sphere of radius 0.13 (#E8622A) labeled q just below-left. Helix: axis is the x-axis line, centered on it; default loop radius 1.0 world unit in the y–z plane, 3 full turns, pitch ≈ 1.2 units, first turn centered near x = 1.5 so the coils occupy roughly x = 1.0 to 4.6 — i.e. the coils sit to the RIGHT of the particle, filling the right half of the frame, and the loops visibly overlap on screen. Helix stroke orange #E8622A, line width ~2. Arrowheads at ~2 points per turn giving counter-clockwise sense when viewed from +x looking back toward the origin. Velocity vectors originate at the particle: v_perp green (#4C9A2A / #6AA84F) length 1.5 straight up +Y, labeled to its left; v_para green length ~0.7 along +X labeled below the axis; resultant v⃗ green length ~1.6 tilted so it lies between them (about 55–65° above the x-axis, slightly toward +Z). F⃗ red (#CC2A1E) length ~0.8 from the particle pointing up-and-right into the coil region (direction of qv_perp×B). B⃗ blue (#2A6FD6) arrow along +X from about x=1.6 to x=2.8, drawn on the axis, labeled below its tip. Green double-headed pitch arrow (#6AA84F) drawn above the coils at about y = +1.4, spanning exactly one pitch in x, labeled 'v_para'. Physics: set q=m=B=1 so gyroradius r = v_perp, angular frequency ω = qB/m = 1 (independent of speed), period T = 2π, pitch = v_para·T = 2π·v_para scaled so default v_para=0.8 yields the ~1.2-unit drawn pitch. Background white, labels dark gray/black serif-italic vector notation.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the helix as a THREE.Line from a parametric curve p(t) = (v_para·t, r·cos(ωt), r·sin(ωt)) sampled at ~400 points; regenerate (or scale a cached tube) live when either slider changes so the learner sees the pitch/radius respond instantly. Use TubeGeometry only if arrowheads are added as separate small cone meshes placed at chosen t values. Vectors: cylinder shaft + cone head grouped, or ArrowHelper with setLength on slider change. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/sprite HTML so italic vector notation renders crisply and stays upright while orbiting. The animated particle advances t at constant rate; leave a fading trail via a second Line whose drawRange grows. Keep the axes as thin dark lines with cone arrowheads; draw them with depthTest off so they stay visible through the coils, as in the source line drawing. Default camera: standard isometric pose so z projects to lower-left and x to the right, matching the figure.

authoredContext:
The result is a helical motion, as shown in the following figure.

A charged particle moving with a velocity not in the same direction as the magnetic field. The velocity component perpendicular to the magnetic field creates circular motion, whereas the component of the velocity parallel to the field moves the particle along a straight line. The pitch is the horizontal distance between two consecutive circles. The resulting motion is helical.

An illustration of a positively charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. The field is in the positive x direction. The initial velocity is shown as having a component, v sub para, in the positive x direction and another component, v sub perp, in the positive y direction. The particle moves in a helix that loops in the y z plane (counterclockwise from the particle’s perspective) and advances in the positive x direction.

While the charged particle travels in a helical path, it may enter a region where the magnetic field is not uniform. In particular, suppose a particle travels from a region of strong magnetic field to a region of weaker field, then back to a region of stronger field. The particle may reflect back before entering the stronger magnetic field region. This is similar to a wave on a string traveling from a very light, thin string to a hard wall and reflecting backward. If the reflection happens at both ends, the particle is trapped in a so-called magnetic bottle.

discrepancies: Camera framing differs: in the source the x-axis runs horizontally across the page with y vertical and z receding lower-left, whereas the generated view tilts the x-axis ~30° downward to the right, so the helix marches diagonally down-right instead of straight across — recognizable but noticeably different composition.
The scene occupies only a small central portion of the canvas (large empty margins), making the figure much smaller relative to the frame than the source, where the helix and axes fill the image.

The helix starts at x = 1.0 and its first loop sits clearly away from the vector cluster; in the source the first coil overlaps the origin region so that the v, v_perp, v_para and F arrows sit inside/next to the first loop.
Control-panel slider captions wrap awkwardly ('v', '∥', '(along', 'B', '):' each on its own line), degrading readability of the interaction labels (figure labels themselves are fine).

Source draws the coils as thin orange outlines of roughly equal apparent size with only a couple of directional arrowheads; the generated version adds six cone arrowheads along the tube, slightly busier than the original.

discrepancies: The camera looks almost straight down the z-axis: the z-axis arrow collapses to a tiny black stub near the origin (only its label identifies it), whereas the source shows a full-length z arrow running to the lower-left.

Because F points along −z, the red force arrow is foreshortened into a small red blob beside the charge — in the source it is a clearly visible red arrow labelled F, one of the key pedagogical elements.

Coil aspect ratio and spacing differ: the source shows three nearly-overlapping, wide ellipses hugging the origin; the generated helix has widely separated, narrow (strongly horizontally compressed) loops spread far along +x, so the trajectory reads as a stretched spring rather than the compact coil cluster of the source.
The source has a single arrowhead on the coil indicating the sense of gyration; the generated figure adds two, and the helix starts offset along +x rather than emerging from the charge at O.
The x-axis is drawn slightly tilted (not horizontal) and the overall vector cluster (v, v_perp, v_para) sits smaller relative to the helix than in the source.
evaluation.notes: Physics, colour scheme, and labelling are faithful and the interaction set (two sliders, launch animation, 5-step guided demo, clickable annotated parts) is excellent, but the chosen viewpoint nearly looks down z so the z-axis and the crucial red F vector degenerate into stubs and the coils are over-compressed/over-spread relative to the printed figure.

feedback.rationale: The concept, physics, and interaction structure are correct; the issues are execution details (camera angle collapsing the z-axis and F vector, helix proportions/start point, extra arrowhead, tilted x-axis) that require rendering fixes rather than a new plan.

Axis labels 'x', 'y', 'z' at arrow tips and 'O' at the origin
Small orange sphere (the charge) at the origin, labeled 'q' just below it
Green arrow v_perp pointing straight up along +y from the particle, labeled 'v⃗_perp'

interactions.teaches: The helix is a circle in the y–z plane carried steadily along x; rotating the view shows the trajectory is truly three-dimensional, not a wavy 2D curve.
The perpendicular velocity component makes the particle circle the field line while the parallel component carries it forward at constant speed, producing a helix.
interactions.label: Launch particle

interactions.teaches: Increasing the velocity component along B stretches the pitch (spacing between turns) while leaving the loop radius and rotation period unchanged.
interactions.label: v_parallel (along B)

interactions.teaches: The perpendicular component sets the gyroradius r = m·v_perp/(qB) and the tangential speed, but never the axial advance per turn's period.
interactions.label: v_perpendicular (across B)

demo_steps.title: Velocity split into two components
demo_steps.narration: The charge q at the origin has velocity v⃗ oblique to B⃗, which points along +x. Decompose it: v_perp up along y, v_para along x.

demo_steps.title: Perpendicular part alone → circle
demo_steps.narration: With v_para set to zero, the magnetic force F = qv×B stays perpendicular to the motion and the particle traces a closed circle in the plane perpendicular to B.

demo_steps.title: Add forward motion → helix
demo_steps.narration: Restoring v_para carries the circling particle steadily along the field line; the circle becomes a helix whose pitch is v_para times the cyclotron period.

demo_steps.title: Stretching the pitch
demo_steps.narration: Doubling v_para doubles the spacing between turns while the loop radius stays exactly the same — forward speed alone sets the pitch.

demo_steps.title: Widening the gyration
demo_steps.narration: Raising v_perp enlarges the loop radius and the speed around it, but the period — and therefore the pitch — is unchanged.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: +X is screen-right (the x-axis and B direction), +Y is screen-up, +Z recedes toward the lower-left. x-axis drawn from -0.8 to +6.0 with arrowhead at right; y-axis from 0 to +3.2; z-axis from 0 to about +2.0 projected toward lower-left (shorter than the others). Origin O at world (0,0,0) with an orange sphere of radius 0.13 (#E8622A) labeled q just below-left. Helix: axis is the x-axis line, centered on it; default loop radius 1.0 world unit in the y–z plane, 3 full turns, pitch ≈ 1.2 units, first turn centered near x = 1.5 so the coils occupy roughly x = 1.0 to 4.6 — i.e. the coils sit to the RIGHT of the particle, filling the right half of the frame, and the loops visibly overlap on screen. Helix stroke orange #E8622A, line width ~2. Arrowheads at ~2 points per turn giving counter-clockwise sense when viewed from +x looking back toward the origin. Velocity vectors originate at the particle: v_perp green (#4C9A2A / #6AA84F) length 1.5 straight up +Y, labeled to its left; v_para green length ~0.7 along +X labeled below the axis; resultant v⃗ green length ~1.6 tilted so it lies between them (about 55–65° above the x-axis, slightly toward +Z). F⃗ red (#CC2A1E) length ~0.8 from the particle pointing up-and-right into the coil region (direction of qv_perp×B). B⃗ blue (#2A6FD6) arrow along +X from about x=1.6 to x=2.8, drawn on the axis, labeled below its tip. Green double-headed pitch arrow (#6AA84F) drawn above the coils at about y = +1.4, spanning exactly one pitch in x, labeled 'v_para'. Physics: set q=m=B=1 so gyroradius r = v_perp, angular frequency ω = qB/m = 1 (independent of speed), period T = 2π, pitch = v_para·T = 2π·v_para scaled so default v_para=0.8 yields the ~1.2-unit drawn pitch. discrepancies: Helix proportions differ: the source shows three nearly-coincident, tightly stacked loops of large radius hugging the origin, while the generated helix has a much larger pitch-to-radius ratio and stretches far down the +x axis like an extended spring, changing the figure's silhouette at a glance.

The red F arrow is very short and stubby compared with the source, where it is a clearly visible arrow of comparable length to the velocity components; it also reads as a small red blob near the origin rather than a labelled vector.

The green v_para arrow along +x is barely visible (very short and partly buried under the x-axis and charge sphere), whereas in the source it is a distinct green arrow with a clear head below the axis.
Coil/loop radius is noticeably smaller relative to the axes than in the source, so the loops no longer visually reach up near the v_perp arrow tip as in the original.
The blue B arrow sits deeper inside the coil region (x=1.6–2.8) and is partially occluded by the orange tube, unlike the source where it is cleanly drawn near the first loop.
evaluation.notes: A conceptually correct, well-labelled and richly interactive rendition of the helical-motion figure, but the helix is drawn with an exaggerated pitch and smaller radius (plus a stubby F and nearly invisible v_para), so it reads as a stretched spring rather than the tight overlapping loops of the source.
action_items: Reduce the default pitch (or increase loop radius) so the three turns overlap tightly near the origin as in the source, and keep the drawn helix within roughly the same x-extent as the original figure.
Lengthen and thicken the red F arrow and the green v_para arrow so both are clearly visible as distinct vectors with their labels adjacent, not overlapping the axis/charge sphere.
Move the blue B arrow to a less occluded x range (or raise its render order) so the vector and its label stand out from the orange tube as in the source.
Slightly increase label font sizes for the primary vector labels (v, v_perp, v_para, F, B) to establish a hierarchy over the axis labels, matching the source's bold vector annotations.
